surfaces.part: flat ground tile texture (earth patches and grey-brown speckle)

answer.evidence: This is a seamless terrain tile, 64x48 px fully opaque. The columns show repeating dark 1-2 row lines at a 16-row period (rows 9-10, 25-26, 41-42), which are small dark pebble and crack marks in the texture and not front-edge lines. There is no front face, eave, ellipse or roof, so it reads as a flat top-down ground texture. That is correct for the terrain kind, so no standing-object structure is expected.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a seamless-looking soil patch with no outline, which suits a ground tile. It shows 8 visible tones per 16x16 tile, against 3 for the grass reference and 7 for the paving reference. Near-flat coverage is 0%, so there are no flat fills. Grey-brown base, darker brown speckle and rust-orange streaks give about 5 distinct lightness steps, and the grain is scattered and varied. It is a little less structured than the grass reference's clumps and tufts, but the tones and grain are comparable to the references. Dark edge pixels are 0% neutral, so any darker pixels carry a brown tint rather than a sticker-like black line.

surfaces.part: ground tile surface (flat earth texture with pebbles and dark patches)

answer.evidence: The candidate is a full-bleed 64x48 flat ground texture. The silhouette is a uniform 64 wide for every row, with no outline, no front face and no standing volume. The column scan shows repeating 16-row patterns of brown and grey earth with small dark crack lines, which are texture, not edge lines or eave shadows. It is a seamless terrain tile and has no object structure, so it reads as a flat top-down surface.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a ground patch with grey-brown earth and rust-brown speckle, so it matches the grass and paving references in kind. Measured facts: 8 visible tones per tile, above the grass reference (3) and the paving reference (7), with 0% near-flat coverage and 0% neutral dark edge pixels. The picture is less convincing. It has only about 4 lightness steps (grey base, lighter grey flecks, rust patches, dark brown dashes). The raw count is only 8-9 colours, against 26 per tile on the grass reference. The rust dabs and dashes are scattered fairly evenly and read as noise, not as shaded clods, cracks or grain clusters. Nothing is outlined, which is fine for ground. It lacks the structured tufts and per-stone shading that make the references read as crafted, so it looks a little thinner and flatter than they do. It is not a flat fill, but I am not confident a careful artist would put it next to the references unchanged.
